title: Mount Carmel
lead: Carmel, "garden land," is the green ridge running to the sea at Haifa. It is the scene of Elijah's contest with the prophets of Baal, and a byword for beauty and fruitfulness in the prophets and the Song of Songs.

sections.b: The ridge marked the border of Asher (Joshua 19:26). Its rich growth made it a symbol: when the LORD roars, "the shepherds' meadows go dry, and Carmel's summit withers" (Amos 1:2, in a fresh rendering); in the new age "Lebanon's glory is given to it, and the beauty of Carmel and of Sharon" (Isaiah 35:2); the beloved's head is "like Carmel" (Song of Songs 7:5). Elijah's contest takes place there (1 Kings 18:19–46), and Elisha later lives there for a time (2 Kings 2:25; 2 Kings 4:25). The Roman historian Tacitus knew Carmel as both a mountain and a god, with an altar but no image (Histories 2.78). The Carmelite order takes its name from hermits who lived there in the Middle Ages, and Christian tradition places the contest at el-Muhraqa, "the place of burning." This is a different place from the town of Carmel in Judah, Nabal's home (1 Samuel 25:2).
